- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/05/30 (Tue) 17:01
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The policy of unrestricted submarine warfare was a naval warfare strategy used by Germany during World War I.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The policy involved German submarines, known as U-boats, attacking any and all ships, including civilian vessels, that entered waters around Britain and other parts of Europe.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] This was in contrast to the previously used "cruiser rules," which required submarines to surface and allow crew and passengers to abandon ship before being sunk.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The German government declared unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1915, in response to the British naval blockade that was strangling the German economy.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The goal of the policy was to disrupt the flow of supplies to Britain and its allies and to force them to negotiate a peace settlement.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Unrestricted submarine warfare led to a significant increase in the number of ships sunk, including many neutral vessels.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The sinking of the British passenger liner RMS Lusitania in May 1915 resulted in the deaths of over 1,000 people, including 128 Americans, leading to widespread international outrage and pressure on Germany to change its policy.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] In response to diplomatic pressure, Germany suspended unrestricted submarine warfare in September 1915, but resumed it in February 1917.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Germany hoped to win the war before the United States could enter on the side of the Allies, but this decision ultimately contributed to the United States entering the war in April 1917.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] In summary, the policy of unrestricted submarine warfare was a naval warfare strategy used by Germany during World War I, involving attacking any and all ships to disrupt the flow of supplies to Britain and its allies.
- [USER] asked where the policy of unrestricted submarine warfare was written.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The policy was declared by Germany as a government policy rather than being formally written down in a specific document or treaty.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The German government made public statements announcing the policy and its intentions, which were widely understood by both the German Navy and its opponents.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The policy was first declared in February 1915 by Germany's Admiral von Tirpitz.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The decision was made in response to the British naval blockade that was strangling the German economy.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The policy was later suspended in response to diplomatic pressure but was resumed in February 1917.
